definition: The lowest or worst point in the course of something, such as a career or a season.
example: The team reached its nadir in March, losing nine games in a row before the coach changed its lineup.
nuance: Nadir is the opposite of zenith; it names the single lowest point of a decline, not just any bad stretch or the bottom of an object.
prompt: A small bakery struggled through a hard year before business finally recovered.
options: The bakery hit its nadir in February, when just three customers came all week.
Customers praised the bakery's nadir, a crowded week when every shelf sold out.
The owner's nadir was to open a second location by the following spring.
The baker added a nadir of salt to each loaf to sharpen the flavor.
reasons: The emptiest week marks the worst moment before the recovery, so the word fits.
A sold-out, crowded week is a high point, which reverses the word's meaning.
The word names a low point, not a goal or plan someone aims for.
The word does not mean a small amount; it marks the worst stage of something.

practice.prompt: A student looks back over his grades during a difficult school year.
options: His teacher awarded him a nadir for turning in every essay a week early.
His grades hit their nadir in November, then rose once he joined a study group.
His nadir was the straight-A report card he proudly brought home at the end of June.
He finally found his lost calculator at the nadir of his crowded backpack.
reasons: The word is not a prize or reward; it describes a time when things are at their worst.
November was his worst point before things improved, which is exactly the sense intended.
Perfect grades are a peak, the opposite of the lowest point.
The word describes the low point of a course or decline, not the physical bottom of a bag.
